SECTION 1 · WHAT PENETRATION TESTING IS
Why This Field Exists: The Current Threat Landscape
20%
of breaches in the 2025 Verizon DBIR began
with the exploitation of a vulnerability, a 34%
increase on the previous year.
30%
of breaches involved a third party such as a
vendor or supplier, double the share reported
the year before.
44%
of breaches involved ransomware, which rises
to 88% of breaches at small and medium-
sized businesses.
$4.44M
was the global average cost of a data breach
in IBM's 2025 report; the U.S. average
reached $10.22 million.
241 days
was the average time organizations needed to
identify and contain a breach, the lowest
figure in nine years.
12,195
confirmed data breaches were analysed in
the 2025 DBIR, drawn from more than
22,000 security incidents.
The lesson is simple: attackers are actively looking for weaknesses, so organizations need someone friendly to find those weaknesses first.
Sources: Verizon 2025 Data Breach Investigations Report; IBM Cost of a Data Breach Report 2025.
04
SECTION 1 · WHAT PENETRATION TESTING IS
Defining Penetration Testing
NIST DEFINITION
"Security testing in which evaluators mimic real-
world attacks in an attempt to identify ways to
circumvent the security features of an
application, system, or network."
NIST Computer Security Resource Center glossary, based on NIST
SP 800-115
Four elements make a test a penetration test
• Authorized: The asset owner has given written permission, and the testing
stays inside an agreed scope and set of rules.
• Adversarial: The tester uses the same tools, techniques and creativity a
real attacker would use, rather than only checking boxes.
• Proven: Weaknesses are actually exploited, safely and within limits, to
demonstrate real-world impact instead of theoretical risk.
• Constructive: The engagement ends with a report that explains every
finding, its business impact and how to fix it.
Ethical hacking is the broader umbrella term for any authorized hacking; a
penetration test is a structured, scoped and time-boxed engagement under
that umbrella.

SECTION 1 · WHAT PENETRATION TESTING IS
Why Organizations Pay for Penetration Testing
Risk reduction
Testing finds exploitable weaknesses before criminals do, and it ranks
them by real-world impact so that limited budgets are spent on the
fixes that matter most.
Compliance
Standards such as PCI DSS require penetration testing outright, while
others such as GDPR, SOC 2 and ISO/IEC 27001 expect regular
testing as evidence of effective controls.
Assurance
An independent report gives boards, customers, partners and cyber-
insurance providers evidence that security controls actually work, not
just that they exist on paper.
Due diligence
Testing before a product launch, a merger or a new vendor
relationship shows that leaders took reasonable care, which matters
to regulators, courts and investors after an incident.
Additional benefits: a test validates the return on security investments, trains defenders by showing them real attack techniques, and creates a baseline
that later tests can be measured against.
Penetration Testing · Week 1 · Introduction to Penetration Testing & Lab Foundations
07
SECTION 1 · WHAT PENETRATION TESTING IS
Who Performs Penetration Tests
Internal teams
Employees who test their own organization
know its systems and business deeply and
can test continuously as things change.
Watch for: Familiarity can create blind spots,
and some standards require testers to be
organizationally independent from the
systems they test.
Consultancies
External firms provide independent, certified
specialists who bring fresh eyes and
experience from many different client
environments.
Watch for: Engagements are time-boxed
and costly, and testers start with less context
about how the business really works.
Bug bounty programs
Organizations invite many independent
researchers, often through platforms such as
HackerOne or Bugcrowd, and pay only for
valid, in-scope findings.
Watch for: Coverage is uneven because
researchers chase rewards, so a bounty
complements a structured test rather than
replacing it.
Many mature organizations combine all three: an internal team for continuous testing, an annual independent test for assurance, and a bounty or
vulnerability disclosure program for ongoing coverage.
Penetration Testing · Week 1 · Introduction to Penetration Testing & Lab Foundations

SECTION 1 · WHAT PENETRATION TESTING IS
Thinking Like an Attacker: CIA vs. DAD
DEFENDER'S GOALS · CIA
Confidentiality: Only authorized people can read the
information.
Integrity: Information and systems are not changed without
authorization.
Availability: Systems and data are accessible when legitimate
users need them.
ATTACKER'S GOALS · DAD
Disclosure: The attacker exposes data, which defeats
confidentiality.
Alteration: The attacker modifies data or systems, which
defeats integrity.
Denial: The attacker disrupts access, which defeats
availability.
• Defenders must protect every possible entry point, while an attacker needs to find only one that works; testers adopt that attacker's perspective on
purpose.
• Every finding in a report should explain which part of the DAD triad it enables, because that is how technical issues are translated into business impact.

ACTIVITY 1 · PAIRS · 8 MINUTES
Which Service Does This Client Need?
For each client below, choose the best-fit service from the four options and write one sentence that justifies your choice.
Vulnerability assessment
Penetration test
Red team engagement
Bug bounty program
1. A small dental clinic wants an affordable list of missing patches across its 25 workstations, repeated every quarter.
2. An online retailer must prove to its card processor that an internet attacker cannot reach cardholder data, and needs evidence that any weaknesses
found are truly exploitable.
3. A bank with a mature 24/7 security operations centre wants to know whether its analysts would detect a stealthy, months-long attack; only the CISO
will be told.
4. A popular software-as-a-service company wants continuous testing of its public web application by many independent researchers and wants to pay
only for valid findings.
5. A hospital wants to know, before go-live, whether an attacker could chain flaws in its new patient portal to view other patients' records.
Bonus question: Why is a vulnerability scan on its own never considered a penetration test?
Penetration Testing · Week 1 · Introduction to Penetration Testing & Lab Foundations
10
ACTIVITY 1 · SOLUTION
Matching Each Client to the Right Service
#
Best fit
Why
1
Vulnerability assessment
The clinic needs breadth, low cost and repetition rather than proof of exploitation, which is exactly what
scheduled scanning provides.
2
Penetration test
The retailer needs proof that weaknesses are exploitable, and PCI DSS Requirement 11.4 explicitly
requires penetration testing.
3
Red team engagement
The goal is to test detection and response by a mature SOC, and keeping defenders unaware is a defining
feature of red teaming.
4
Bug bounty program
Continuous coverage by many researchers, paid per valid finding, is the bug bounty model.
5
Penetration test
"Chaining flaws" means proving how far an attacker can go, and a gray- or white-box application test
before launch fits best.
Bonus answer: A scan only reports that a weakness might exist. Nothing is exploited, so the scan cannot prove impact, cannot show how
weaknesses chain together and often includes false positives that a human must validate.

SECTION 2 · REGULATORY & COMPLIANCE DRIVERS
PCI DSS v4.0.1: Testing Is Mandatory
WHO IT APPLIES TO
The Payment Card Industry Data Security
Standard applies to every organization
that stores, processes or transmits
payment card data, or that can affect the
security of that data.
It is a contractual standard enforced by
the card brands and banks, not a
government law, but non-compliance can
lead to fines and loss of the ability to
accept cards.
11.4.1 · A documented methodology must follow an industry-accepted approach and cover the whole
cardholder data environment, from inside and outside, at the network and application layers.
11.4.2 / 11.4.3 · Internal and external penetration tests must be performed at least once every 12
months and after any significant change.
11.4.4 · Exploitable vulnerabilities must be corrected, and testing must be repeated to verify the fixes.
11.4.5 / 11.4.6 · Network segmentation controls must be tested every 12 months, or every six months
for service providers.
Tester · A qualified internal resource or third party may test, provided they are organizationally
independent of the systems tested.
PCI DSS also requires separate quarterly vulnerability scans (Requirement 11.3), with external scans performed by an Approved Scanning Vendor.
Source: PCI Security Standards Council, PCI DSS v4.0.1 (June 2024), Requirements 11.3 and 11.4.
12
SECTION 2 · REGULATORY & COMPLIANCE DRIVERS
HIPAA and GDPR: Testing Expected by Law
HIPAA Security Rule (United States)
• HIPAA applies to health plans, healthcare providers, healthcare
clearinghouses and their business associates that handle electronic
protected health information.
• The current rule requires a risk analysis and a periodic technical
evaluation of safeguards, but it does not name penetration testing
explicitly.
• A January 2025 proposed rule would require vulnerability scans
every six months and penetration tests every 12 months.
• That proposal is not yet final; regulators currently project final action
for July 2027.
GDPR (European Union)
• GDPR applies to any organization, anywhere in the world, that
processes the personal data of people in the EU.
• Article 32(1)(d) requires "a process for regularly testing, assessing
and evaluating the effectiveness" of security measures.
• The regulation does not prescribe a method, so penetration testing is
a common way to demonstrate that testing took place.
• Breaches of Article 32 can bring fines of up to €10 million or 2% of
worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher.
Sources: 45 CFR §164.308; HHS NPRM, 90 FR 898 (6 Jan 2025); McDermott Will & Schaumburg (2026); GDPR Arts. 32 and 83(4).
13
SECTION 2 · REGULATORY & COMPLIANCE DRIVERS
SOC 2, ISO/IEC 27001 and the Canadian Context
SOC 2
SOC 2 is an independent audit report on a
service organization's controls, based on the
AICPA Trust Services Criteria.
No law requires it, but enterprise customers
often demand it, and auditors commonly
expect annual penetration test results as
evidence for the monitoring criteria.
ISO/IEC 27001:2022
ISO/IEC 27001 is an international
certification for an information security
management system.
Annex A controls 8.8 (management of
technical vulnerabilities) and 8.29 (security
testing in development and acceptance) are
usually evidenced with scans and penetration
tests.
Canada and B.C.
PIPEDA's safeguards principle and B.C.'s
PIPA (section 34) require security that is
reasonable and appropriate to the sensitivity
of personal information.
OSFI Guideline B-13 expects federally
regulated financial institutions to test
regularly, explicitly naming penetration
testing and red teaming.
Sources: AICPA Trust Services Criteria; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A; PIPEDA Sch. 1, 4.7; B.C. PIPA s.34; OSFI Guideline B-13, s.3.1.2.

SECTION 3 · TEAMS & ENGAGEMENT TYPES
Red, Blue, Purple and White Teams
Red team · the attackers
The red team plays the adversary, using offensive techniques to achieve
agreed objectives such as reaching sensitive data, often while trying to
avoid detection.
Blue team · the defenders
The blue team protects the organization day to day, monitoring alerts in
the security operations centre, hardening systems and responding to
incidents.
Purple team · the collaboration
Purple teaming is a way of working in which red and blue share results in
real time, so each attack immediately becomes an improved detection
or control.
White team · the referees
The white team sets the rules of engagement, oversees the exercise,
resolves disputes and can stop testing immediately if something goes
wrong.
A penetration tester is usually part of a red team or works in a red-team role; in this course you will practise both the attacker's techniques and the
defender's view of the same activity.
Penetration Testing · Week 1 · Introduction to Penetration Testing & Lab Foundations

SECTION 3 · TEAMS & ENGAGEMENT TYPES
Delivery Models and Assessment Types
External vs. internal
An external test starts from the internet and targets public-facing systems; an
internal test starts inside the network and asks what an insider or a
compromised device could reach.
On-site vs. remote
Testers either work at the client's premises or connect remotely, often through a
VPN or a small device the client installs on its network.
Announced vs. unannounced
In an announced test, IT staff know testing is happening; in an unannounced
test, only a few leaders know, so the real response of the defenders is
measured.
ASSESSMENT TYPES
Compliance-based: The test is designed to satisfy a specific
standard, such as PCI DSS, and follows its required scope and
method.
Goal-based: The test pursues a defined objective, such as
reaching the customer database, using whatever in-scope path
works.
Red-team: The test emulates a realistic adversary over a longer
period to measure detection and response.

ACTIVITY 3 · SOLUTION
Engagement Designs Explained
#
Recommended design
Reasoning
1
Black box, external, unannounced, goal-based
An anonymous outsider has no inside knowledge, and not warning IT staff also
measures their response.
2
White box, application test, announced
Sharing source code allows the most thorough review before launch, when fixes
are cheapest.
3
Gray box, internal, announced, standard user account
The concern is what a normal employee can reach, so the test starts inside with
that level of access.
4
Purple team exercise, announced, gray or white box
Real-time collaboration between testers and defenders is the definition of purple
teaming.
Discussion answer: An unannounced test needs a "trusted agent" or white-team contact who knows about the test, can confirm that alerts are
part of the exercise, and can stop testing at once. The authorization letter must also be signed by someone with authority over the systems.

SECTION 4 · STAGE 1 OF 4
Stage 1: Planning and Scoping
• Goals: The client and tester agree what the test must answer, such as whether
customer data can be reached from the internet.
• Scope: The documents list exactly which systems, addresses, applications and
locations are in scope, and which are explicitly out of scope.
• Rules of engagement: The rules define permitted techniques, testing hours,
contacts, how to report urgent findings and how to stop testing immediately.
• Contracts and authorization: A statement of work, a non-disclosure agreement
and a signed authorization letter make the testing legal.
Outputs of this stage
A signed statement of work that defines deliverables, dates
and cost.
A written scope and rules of engagement approved by the
client.
A signed authorization letter from someone with authority over
the systems.
Covered in depth in Week 2.
Penetration Testing · Week 1 · Introduction to Penetration Testing & Lab Foundations
24
SECTION 4 · STAGE 2 OF 4
Stage 2: Information Gathering and Vulnerability Scanning
Passive reconnaissance
The tester collects publicly available
information without directly contacting the
target, such as domain records, job postings
and public certificate logs.
Active reconnaissance
The tester interacts with in-scope systems to
discover which hosts are live, which services
they run and which versions are installed.
Vulnerability scanning
Scanners compare discovered services
against databases of known weaknesses, and
the tester then validates results to remove
false positives.
OUTPUTS
An inventory of in-scope assets, a map of the attack surface, and a
validated, prioritized list of potential vulnerabilities.
EXAMPLE TOOLS
theHarvester, Recon-ng, Shodan and whois for passive work; Nmap for
active discovery; Greenbone OpenVAS and Nikto for scanning.
Penetration Testing · Week 1 · Introduction to Penetration Testing & Lab Foundations
25
SECTION 4 · STAGE 3 OF 4
Stage 3: Attacks and Exploits
• Exploitation: The tester attempts to use validated weaknesses, within the rules
of engagement, to prove that they are real and to show their impact.
• Post-exploitation: The tester assesses what the access allows, such as higher
privileges or reaching other systems, and how far an attacker could progress.
• Attack areas covered this term: networks and wireless, web applications, people
through social engineering, specialized systems and cloud services.
• Clean-up: Any test accounts, files or changes created during testing are removed,
and anything that cannot be removed is reported to the client.
Professional safeguards
The tester stays strictly within scope and stops to ask
whenever something is unclear.
Techniques that could disrupt production systems are used
only when the rules of engagement allow them.
Every action is logged with a timestamp, and sensitive data is
accessed only to the extent needed as proof.
Penetration Testing · Week 1 · Introduction to Penetration Testing & Lab Foundations
26
SECTION 4 · STAGE 4 OF 4
Stage 4: Reporting and Communication
The written report
• An executive summary explains the overall risk in plain business
language for leaders.
• A methodology and scope section records what was tested, how and
when.
• Each finding includes a description, a risk rating such as a CVSS score,
evidence, business impact and clear remediation steps.
• An appendix holds supporting technical detail, tool output and the
clean-up record.
Communication throughout
• Regular status updates keep the client informed about progress and
any issues.
• Critical findings are escalated immediately rather than waiting for the
final report.
• Signs of a previous or ongoing real attack are reported at once to the
agreed contact.
• A debrief presents results to stakeholders, and a retest confirms that
fixes work.
The report is the only part of the engagement the client keeps, so its clarity and accuracy determine the value of the entire test.
Penetration Testing · Week 1 · Introduction to Penetration Testing & Lab Foundations
27
SECTION 4 · THE FOUR-STAGE PROCESS
How the Stages Feed One Another
• The scope agreed in Stage 1 limits every action in Stages 2 and 3, so testers check it
continually rather than once.
• The validated vulnerability list from Stage 2 becomes the plan of attack for Stage 3.
• New access gained in Stage 3 often reveals systems that were not visible before, which
sends the tester back to Stage 2 to gather information about them, provided they are in
scope.
• Notes, screenshots and timestamps collected from the first day become the evidence in
Stage 4, so reporting starts at the beginning, not the end.
ACME CORP · MINI-ENGAGEMENT
1 · The scope lists the lab network 192.168.56.0/24.
2 · Discovery finds a server running an outdated file-
transfer service with a published vulnerability.
3 · Testing confirms the weakness gives administrator
access and reveals a reused database password.
2 again · That password points to a second in-scope
server, so information gathering resumes there.
4 · The report links the chain to two root causes:
missing patches and password reuse.
Penetration Testing · Week 1 · Introduction to Penetration Testing & Lab Foundations
28
ACTIVITY 4 · SMALL GROUPS · 10 MINUTES
Which Stage Would Have Caught It?
For each real breach, decide which stage of a penetration test would most likely have revealed the weakness first, and name one recommendation
the report should have made.
1. Equifax (2017): A web portal ran a version of Apache Struts with a known, published vulnerability for about two months after a fix was available; data on
about 147 million people was exposed.
2. Capital One (2019): A misconfigured web application firewall in the cloud allowed an outsider to obtain credentials and read stored data on about 100 million
U.S. and 6 million Canadian customers.
3. MGM Resorts (2023): Attackers used public information about an employee to phone the IT help desk, impersonate that employee and obtain account
access.
4. Target (2013): Attackers used credentials stolen from a heating and air-conditioning vendor and moved from vendor-facing systems to payment terminals.
5. Colonial Pipeline (2021): Attackers logged in through an old VPN account that was still active and was not protected by multi-factor authentication.

ACTIVITY 4 · SOLUTION
Mapping Real Breaches to the Four Stages
Breach
Stage that would reveal it
Key report recommendation
Equifax
Stage 2: scanning flags the known vulnerable version; Stage 3
confirms it.
Patch critical vulnerabilities quickly and keep a complete asset
inventory.
Capital One
Stage 3: testing the cloud application shows how settings
combine into access.
Review cloud configurations and limit the permissions given to
each role.
MGM Resorts
Stage 2 shows exposed staff details; Stage 3 social engineering
tests the help desk.
Require strong identity checks before resetting any credentials.
Target
Stage 3: post-exploitation shows movement from vendor
access to payment systems.
Segment networks and restrict vendor access; include third parties
in scope.
Colonial Pipeline
Stage 2 finds the remote access portal; Stage 3 shows the
account lacks MFA.
Remove unused accounts and require MFA on all remote access.
Common thread: none of these required unknown techniques; each relied on a known weakness that testing and good follow-up could have found and
fixed.
Sources: U.S. House Oversight Committee (2018); Capital One (2019); CISA AA23-320A; U.S. Senate Commerce Committee (2014);
CISA (2023).
30
SECTION 5 · TOOLKIT, LAB & ETHICS
Kali Linux: The Tester's Workbench
• Kali Linux is a free, Debian-based Linux distribution maintained by OffSec and
designed specifically for penetration testing and security research.
• It includes hundreds of preinstalled security tools, organized in the application
menu by category, from information gathering to reporting.
• Kali is available as an installer, ready-made virtual machines for VirtualBox and
VMware, ARM images, a live USB and Windows Subsystem for Linux.
• The default account is a normal user, not root, and administrative commands
are run with sudo, which reduces the risk of accidental damage.
KALI MENU CATEGORIES
Information Gathering · Vulnerability Analysis · Web Application
Analysis · Database Assessment · Password Attacks · Wireless
Attacks · Reverse Engineering · Exploitation Tools · Sniffing &
Spoofing · Post Exploitation · Forensics · Reporting Tools · Social
Engineering Tools
First steps after import: change the default password and update
the system.

Free Tools Mapped to Each Stage
Stage
Free tools
What they do
1 · Planning
ROE templates, MITRE ATT&CK

2 · Recon
theHarvester, Recon-ng, Shodan
They gather public data on domains, emails and services.
2 · Discovery
Nmap, Wireshark
They find live hosts and open ports and show traffic.
2 · Scanning
Greenbone OpenVAS, Nikto
They check systems against known vulnerability lists.
3 · Web testing
Burp Suite Community, ZAP
They intercept web traffic to test how apps handle input.
3 · Exploitation
Metasploit Framework
It validates known vulnerabilities in a controlled way.
3 · Passwords
Hydra, John the Ripper
They test the strength of passwords and logins.
4 · Reporting
Dradis CE, CherryTree, CVSS
They organize evidence and score finding severity.
Many tools span more than one stage; what matters is choosing the right tool for the task at hand and staying within scope.

SECTION 5 · TOOLKIT, LAB & ETHICS
Ethics, Authorization and the Law
• Canada: Criminal Code section 342.1 makes unauthorized use of a computer
an offence punishable by up to 10 years in prison, and section 430(1.1)
covers mischief in relation to computer data.
• United States: The Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (18 U.S.C. §1030)
criminalizes accessing a computer without authorization or exceeding
authorized access.
• Authorization: Permission must be written and must come from someone
who has the authority over the systems, which may include a cloud or
hosting provider.
• Professional ethics: Testers protect confidentiality, report honestly and
never use access for personal gain.
COURSE RULE · READ ALOUD
No system is ever touched without written authorization and an
agreed scope.
All testing is confined to the isolated lab or explicitly authorized
free platforms.
Social-engineering exercises target only fictional personas or
consenting classmates.
Violations are an academic-integrity matter and potentially a legal
one.
Sources: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, ss. 342.1, 430(1.1); 18 U.S.C. §1030; Focus College Instructor Guide.

Part A · Match each tool to its main stage
Write 1 (Planning), 2 (Information gathering and scanning), 3

a) Nmap · b) theHarvester · c) Greenbone OpenVAS · d)
Metasploit Framework · e) Burp Suite Community · f) John the

Part B · Is this acceptable? Explain why.
1. A student scans a roommate's home router "just to practise", without
asking.
2. During an authorized test, a tester finds a partner company's server that is
not in scope and tests it because it is connected.
3. A tester finds customer card numbers during an authorized test and saves
a copy on a personal laptop.
4. A student completes a TryHackMe room against the platform's own
practice machines.
Penetration Testing · Week 1 · Introduction to Penetration Testing & Lab Foundations
34
ACTIVITY 5 · SOLUTION
Tools, Stages and Ethical Judgement: Answers
Part A
Stage 1: h) MITRE ATT&CK, used to plan which adversary
behaviours to cover.
Stage 2: a) Nmap, b) theHarvester, c) Greenbone OpenVAS and i)
Shodan, which gather information and identify known weaknesses.
Stage 3: d) Metasploit Framework, e) Burp Suite Community and f)
John the Ripper, which actively test weaknesses.
Stage 4: g) Dradis CE, which organizes evidence for the report.
Part B
1 · Not acceptable. There is no authorization; the router's owner never gave
permission.
2 · Not acceptable. It is out of scope and owned by a third party; the tester
must stop and contact the client.
3 · Not acceptable. Sensitive data must be handled as the rules require, with
minimal evidence stored securely, never on a personal device.
4 · Acceptable. The platform owns the machines and explicitly authorizes
practice against them.
Penetration Testing · Week 1 · Introduction to Penetration Testing & Lab Foundations
35
CLOSING
Key Takeaways, Homework and Next Week
Five takeaways
1. A penetration test is an authorized, scoped simulation of real attacks that
proves weaknesses and explains how to fix them.
2. Vulnerability assessments, penetration tests and red team exercises answer
different questions and complement one another.
3. Frameworks such as PCI DSS require testing, while many others expect it as
evidence of effective security.
4. Every engagement follows four stages, and each stage feeds the next in a
repeating cycle.
5. Written authorization and an agreed scope are what separate professional
testing from a crime.
Before Week 2
Read Chapter 1 of the CompTIA PenTest+ Study Guide.
Complete the free TryHackMe room "Pentesting Fundamentals".
Confirm your term-project target and collect the written
authorization template.
Bring your laptop to the practical session, following the separate
lab guide.
Week 2: Planning, scoping, legal concepts and methodologies,
plus Quiz 1.
